questions.q: What does an LLM do at its core?
options: Predicts the next token in a sequence
questions.explain: At scale this simple objective yields summarizing, translating, coding and instruction following.

questions.q: When is a local open-weight model the better fit than a hosted API?
options: Privacy-critical or offline use, or high fixed volume
questions.explain: Hosted APIs suit most products; local models run on your own hardware.

questions.q: Why does the course use the Anthropic API for examples?
options: The concepts (messages, system prompts, tools, streaming) are identical across providers
questions.explain: Everything transfers between providers.

questions.q: What is rule one of LLM development regarding the API key?
options: Never hardcode it; use environment variables
questions.explain: Anyone with the key can spend your credit.

questions.q: Why must you resend the whole conversation in each call?
options: The API is stateless: the model only 'remembers' what is in the request
questions.explain: Alternate user/assistant turns, always ending on a user turn.

questions.q: Where does the system prompt go in the Anthropic API?
options: A top-level system parameter, not a message in the list
questions.explain: In OpenAI's API it's a message with role system; the concept is the same.

questions.q: What is max_tokens?
options: A hard cap on output; generation stops at the limit even mid-sentence
questions.explain: It is not a request for a length.

questions.q: What does the system prompt control?
options: Persona, rules, format and boundaries, treated as more authoritative than user text
questions.explain: It is the highest-leverage line in most LLM apps.

questions.q: What is a good mental test for a prompt?
options: Would a smart new intern produce the right output from it alone, with no chance to ask questions?
questions.explain: State the task, audience, format and constraints.

questions.q: Why wrap data in XML-style tags?
options: The model can't confuse data with instructions, and you can refer to sections by name
questions.explain: It also helps defang injection-like inputs.

questions.q: Why use few-shot examples?
options: Showing input→output pairs pins down format and edge cases better than prose
questions.explain: Showing beats telling.

questions.q: Which prompt is stronger?
options: 'Summarize for busy software engineers in exactly 3 bullets under 20 words, no marketing language'
questions.explain: Vague prompts get vague answers.

questions.q: Why isn't 'ask for JSON and json.loads it' enough in production?
options: It works most of the time, but you may get fences, commentary or wrong types
questions.explain: Production code needs guarantees.

questions.q: What does tolerant extraction do?
options: Strips fences and takes the outermost JSON object before parsing
questions.explain: It's a cheap robustness layer.

questions.q: What does pydantic add beyond parsing?
options: Validation: types, requiredness and constraints against your schema
questions.explain: Parsing proves it's JSON; validation proves it's your JSON.

questions.q: What does the toolkit in this module include?
options: Schema-in-prompt, pydantic validation, retry-on-invalid and native structured-output mode
questions.explain: Each step adds more reliability.

questions.q: What is the crucial mental model of tool calling?
options: Tools run on the provider's servers
The model never runs code; it only emits a structured request and your program executes it
The model executes functions on its own
questions.explain: Your program stays in control of what executes.

questions.q: Why does a tool description matter so much?
options: It is hidden from the model
The model reads it to decide when to use the tool, so say when to call it, not just what it does
questions.explain: enum pins down fixed choices in parameters.

questions.q: Why does the lesson implement safe_eval instead of calling eval()?
options: eval() on model-produced text would execute arbitrary code
questions.explain: Parse arithmetic with an allowed set of operators.

questions.q: What is the tool loop?
options: Request → execute → respond: describe tools, model asks, your code runs it, model uses the result
questions.explain: It is the foundation for agents.

questions.q: Why do naive conversation costs balloon?
options: You re-pay for the whole history on every turn; turn 1 is resent in a 50-turn chat 50 times
questions.explain: input_tokens climbs every turn.

questions.q: What is sliding-window truncation?
options: Keeping only the last N turns
questions.explain: It's simple and predictable.

questions.q: What are the two gotchas when truncating?
options: History must be even-length, and must end with assistant
Never trim system prompts, never trim users
History must still start with a user message, and never cut between a tool_use and its tool_result
questions.explain: Trim at whole-exchange boundaries.

questions.q: What does appending the assistant reply to messages represent?
questions.explain: You are the memory manager because the API is stateless.

questions.q: Why stream?
options: Perceived latency: first words in a few hundred milliseconds instead of waiting 10–30 seconds for the full answer
questions.explain: It also avoids HTTP timeouts on very large outputs.

questions.q: Why print with flush=True when streaming?
options: Without it Python buffers output and the stream appears in bursts
questions.explain: flush defeats buffering.

questions.q: What does get_final_message() return?
options: The complete message with usage and stop_reason after the stream ends
questions.explain: Stream for the user, collect the final message for your program.

questions.q: What does text_stream give you?
options: A convenience over the typed event sequence, yielding plain text chunks
questions.explain: Iterate events when you need thinking indicators or tool-call progress.

questions.q: Which errors should you retry with backoff?
options: RateLimitError (429), server errors (≥500) and connection errors
questions.explain: A 400 will fail forever, so fix the code.

questions.q: Why add random jitter to retries?
options: So a fleet of clients doesn't retry in lockstep
questions.explain: Also honor the server's retry-after header when present.

questions.q: What should you catch instead of string-matching error messages?
questions.explain: For example RateLimitError and APIStatusError.

questions.q: What does a 401 AuthenticationError mean?
options: Bad or missing API key: don't retry, fix the key
questions.explain: PermissionDeniedError (403) means the key lacks access.

questions.q: What is the agent loop?
options: Plan → act (call tools) → observe results → repeat until done
questions.explain: The model drives control flow; your code supplies tools, limits and the transcript.

questions.q: What guardrail keeps loops from running away?
questions.explain: The capstone uses MAX_TOOL_ITERATIONS = 8 per user turn.

questions.q: Why does safe_path confine file access to the workspace?
questions.explain: A model could otherwise request files outside the intended directory.

questions.q: When is an agent the wrong tool?
options: When a simple fixed workflow or a single call would do the job more predictably
questions.explain: The module discusses this explicitly.

questions.q: What does the CLI assistant combine?
options: Tools, streaming, conversation memory with summarization, cost tracking and a golden-prompt eval suite
questions.explain: It's a production-style architecture at miniature scale.

questions.q: Why does config.py use a cheaper SUMMARIZER_MODEL?
options: Summarizing history is a simple task, so a cheaper model saves cost
questions.explain: The main model is claude-sonnet-5; the summarizer is claude-haiku-4-5.

questions.q: What does the system prompt tell the assistant about arithmetic?
options: Use the calculator tool for all arithmetic, never compute in its head
questions.explain: It also says to use save_note for durable facts.

questions.q: What are golden prompts in evals.py?
options: Fixed test prompts with expected behavior, run to catch regressions
questions.explain: They form a small evaluation suite.

questions.q: What is meta-prompting?
options: Asking a strong model to draft a prompt, then refining it against real examples
questions.explain: Treat the output as a first draft and validate it against a labeled eval set.

questions.q: What is prompt chaining?
options: Breaking a complex task into a pipeline of focused calls with narrow jobs and clean outputs
questions.explain: For example summarize, then extract actions, then draft a reply.

questions.q: Why validate a meta-generated prompt before shipping?
options: It is only a reasonable starting point, not gospel
questions.explain: Use a labeled eval set.

questions.q: What do the advanced patterns help manage?
options: Prompt libraries that grow into the hundreds, with self-critique loops and versioning
questions.explain: Versioned prompt libraries keep them maintainable.

questions.q: What does prompt caching let the server do?
options: Reuse an already-processed prefix instead of recomputing it, cutting cost and latency
questions.explain: It helps when a large prefix repeats across calls.

questions.q: How do you mark a cacheable prefix?
options: With cache_control on a block; everything up to and including it is a candidate
questions.explain: It's an ephemeral breakpoint.

questions.q: What is the most important caching rule?
options: Tokens before the breakpoint must be byte-for-byte identical across calls; per-request changes go after it
questions.explain: A date or random request ID before the breakpoint breaks the cache.

questions.q: What do the first and second calls show in usage?
options: First writes the cache (high cache_creation tokens); the second reads it (high cache_read, tiny input_tokens)
questions.explain: Reads are charged at a steep discount.

questions.q: How are images sent to the model?
options: As attachments to the API key
As base64 (or URL) image content blocks alongside text in the messages structure
questions.explain: This avoids a separate OCR pipeline for many tasks.

questions.q: Where should the image block go relative to the text instruction?
options: Before the text, since the model reads blocks in order
questions.explain: Grounding the instruction after the image reduces ambiguity.

questions.q: How should you handle comparing two images?
options: Label them explicitly in text, e.g. 'Image 1 (before):', since the model sees blocks in sequence
Send them in separate calls only
questions.explain: There are no named variables.

questions.q: How are PDFs sent?
options: As a document content block, with the model reading both extracted text and page layout
questions.explain: Useful for tables, forms and scanned pages.

questions.q: When should tools run in parallel?
options: Only when they are independent and safe out-of-order, such as read-only lookups
When they write to the same record
questions.explain: Conflicting side effects should stay serial.

questions.q: Why tighten the tool's JSON Schema?
options: A loose schema lets the model emit valid-but-useless arguments; enums and patterns enforce the constraint
questions.explain: Don't rely on the model to infer constraints from descriptions.

questions.q: What does a pattern like ^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$ enforce?
questions.explain: It's the due_date constraint in the create_ticket example.

questions.q: What is a server-side tool?
options: One the model can invoke without a round trip through your code
A tool that needs no schema
questions.explain: The module covers them alongside parallelism and control over when tools fire.

questions.q: What problem does MCP solve?
options: It standardizes how apps discover and call tools exposed by independent servers, so a tool is written once and reused
questions.explain: Hand-written TOOLS lists don't scale across apps.

questions.q: What are the three kinds of things an MCP server exposes?
questions.explain: Resources are readable data addressed by URI; prompts are parameterized templates.

questions.q: How does the Python SDK's @mcp.tool() build the schema?
options: It inspects the function's type hints and docstring
You write the JSON by hand
questions.explain: You write a normal Python function.

questions.q: How does your app act with MCP?
options: As a client that launches or connects to the server and forwards its tools into messages.create
questions.explain: Servers use stdio for local processes or HTTP for remote ones.

questions.q: What is a golden dataset?
options: A fixed set of representative inputs with known-good outputs, kept in version control
A training set for the model
questions.explain: Include real examples and deliberate edge cases.

questions.q: Why must a golden set include hard cases?
options: A set of only easy cases passes forever and tells you nothing
questions.explain: Use ambiguous inputs, adversarial phrasing and known past failures.

questions.q: When do you score with plain code instead of an LLM?
options: Tasks with a single correct answer, such as classification or extraction
questions.explain: Exact match is meaningless for open-ended output.

questions.q: What is LLM-as-judge?
options: A second model call grades output against a rubric, returning a structured verdict you can aggregate
questions.explain: It's used for open-ended tasks.

questions.q: Why split a planner from an executor?
options: A forced-schema planning call yields a plan you can log, edit or approve before any tool runs, making the agent auditable
questions.explain: The executor only consults the planner again if the plan needs revising.

questions.q: What problem do long-horizon agents hit with a single undifferentiated loop?
options: They drift, lose the original goal or overflow their context window
questions.explain: The patterns here keep them on track.

questions.q: What does tool_choice forcing set_plan guarantee?
options: The model returns a structured plan via that tool
questions.explain: Structured output through a forced tool call.

questions.q: Which patterns does the module cover?
options: Planner/executor splits, reflection, task management and context editing
questions.explain: All aim at long-running tasks.

questions.q: What does the orchestrator do?
options: Decides which subagent handles each piece, delegates via tool calls and assembles the results, without doing the work itself
questions.explain: Subagents are specialized with different roles.

questions.q: Why give subagents distinct abilities and descriptions?
options: The orchestrator reads the tool descriptions to choose the right specialist
questions.explain: For example the researcher can't write code and the coder can't browse.

questions.q: What is a researcher subagent's system prompt told to do?
options: Use only verifiable facts and say clearly when uncertain
questions.explain: Focused instructions per role.

questions.q: When does the orchestrator loop end?
options: When stop_reason is no longer tool_use and the final text is returned
questions.explain: Otherwise it keeps delegating.

questions.q: What is the web framework's job in an LLM web app?
options: Routing and (de)serialization; the LLM logic underneath is unchanged
questions.explain: The /chat endpoint mirrors the terminal conversation loop.

questions.q: Why use Server-Sent Events for streaming?
options: Users see tokens as they're generated instead of staring at a spinner for the full response
questions.explain: The same mechanism as terminal streaming, piped to an HTTP response.

questions.q: Why store history by session_id?
options: A user's conversation persists across requests instead of resetting each time
IDs are required by the API
questions.explain: It's backed by a database.

questions.q: How do you run the FastAPI app in development?
questions.explain: It's then callable from any HTTP client.

questions.q: Which pieces does the agent service combine?
options: FastAPI with SSE, an agent loop with tools and a planner, Redis sessions, a cached system prompt and a CI-gated eval suite
questions.explain: It's the shape of a real production agent.

questions.q: Why cache the system prompt and docs?
options: They are large and stable, so caching cuts cost and latency
questions.explain: Prefix stability is the rule that matters.

questions.q: Why do the tool schemas set additionalProperties: false and minLength?
questions.explain: Module 4's strict schemas.

questions.q: What does the eval.yml workflow do?
options: Gates changes with a regression suite run in CI
questions.explain: Golden prompts catch regressions before shipping.

questions.q: What is a token embedding?
options: A learned vector looked up from an embedding table, not derived from the token's spelling
questions.explain: It's a lookup, shaped by training.

questions.q: Why does a transformer need positional information?
options: Attention has no inherent notion of order, so 'the cat sat' and 'sat cat the' would look identical
questions.explain: A position-dependent vector is added to each embedding.

questions.q: How do rotary position embeddings (RoPE) differ from sinusoidal ones?
options: They rotate query/key vectors by a position-dependent angle, generalizing better to unseen lengths
questions.explain: Modern production models more commonly use RoPE.

questions.q: What does self-attention compute for each token?
options: A weighted average of all tokens' values, with weights from query–key matches
questions.explain: Weights come from how well each query matches every key.

questions.q: Why not tokenize by characters or whole words?
options: Characters make sequences very long; words make the vocabulary explode and can't represent unseen words
questions.explain: BPE sits between them.

questions.q: How does BPE build its vocabulary?
options: Start from characters/bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair
questions.explain: It builds up substrings that actually recur in the corpus.

questions.q: Why can BPE represent any string?
options: Worst case it falls back to individual bytes
questions.explain: Gibberish and new words are still representable.

questions.q: Why do token counts differ between models and strings?
options: Different tokenizers merge different pieces, so strings you expect to cost the same can differ
questions.explain: Token counts drive cost and context use.

questions.q: What problem do embeddings solve over keyword search?
options: Query and document describing the same thing in different words ('car' vs 'automobile')
questions.explain: Similar text lands near each other in vector space.

questions.q: Why use cosine similarity rather than raw distance?
options: It measures the angle, dividing out magnitude, so same-direction vectors are similar regardless of length
questions.explain: cos = a·b / (‖a‖‖b‖).

questions.q: What does input_type (document vs query) do?
options: Models produce slightly different vectors optimized for each role; mixing them degrades search quality without errors
questions.explain: Both calls succeed, which hides the mistake.

questions.q: A query 'How do I get my money back?' matches a doc about refunds. What does that show?
options: Semantic matching works with almost no shared words
questions.explain: That's the value proposition of embeddings.

questions.q: When do you run a model locally with Ollama?
options: Privacy-sensitive data that can't leave your network, offline development, or avoiding per-token cost during heavy experimentation
questions.explain: Hosted APIs remain the faster path to frontier quality.

questions.q: What does the tag in llama3.1:8b select?
options: The parameter count/quantization variant; larger tags need more RAM and are slower but generally more capable
questions.explain: ollama list shows local models.

questions.q: Where does Ollama serve its HTTP API?
options: localhost:11434, with native and OpenAI-compatible endpoints
questions.explain: Switching from a hosted API is mostly a base-URL change.

questions.q: What does "stream": True return?
questions.explain: It mirrors the hosted streaming module.

questions.q: When do you choose vLLM over Ollama?
options: Serving an open-weight model to many concurrent users with production-grade throughput
questions.explain: vLLM uses PagedAttention and continuous batching.

questions.q: Why can client code usually switch to vLLM with only a base_url change?
options: It exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server
questions.explain: The request/response shape matches the hosted OpenAI API.

questions.q: What does PagedAttention do?
options: Splits the KV cache into fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, so memory is used only as tokens are generated and can be shared or freed per block
questions.explain: It borrows OS virtual-memory paging.

questions.q: What was wasteful about naive KV cache allocation?
options: Contiguous memory sized for each request's maximum possible length, unusable by others
questions.explain: Most requests finish well short of the max.

questions.q: When should you try fine-tuning?
options: After prompting (and more few-shot examples) fails to pin down a narrow, high-volume style or format, or to shrink prompt cost/latency
questions.explain: Prompting is cheaper and faster to iterate.

questions.q: Why not use fine-tuning to inject facts?
options: Weights encode patterns, not a queryable knowledge base, and facts go stale once baked in; use retrieval instead
questions.explain: Reserve fine-tuning for behavior and style.

questions.q: What does fine-tuning data look like?
options: (input, ideal-output) pairs in the messages shape; quality and consistency matter far more than volume
questions.explain: Aim for at least a few hundred consistent examples.

questions.q: What does fine-tuning change?
questions.explain: LoRA/QLoRA do this with far fewer trainable parameters.

questions.q: What does quantization do?
options: Stores each weight with fewer bits (8, 4 or fewer), trading precision for a smaller file and faster memory-bound computation
questions.explain: Weights are normally 16- or 32-bit floats.

questions.q: How does symmetric int8 quantization compute its scale?
questions.explain: Quantized = round(w / scale).

questions.q: What is GGUF?
options: The format used by llama.cpp and Ollama, with per-block scaling and several bit-widths, optimized for CPU and consumer GPUs
questions.explain: GGUF, AWQ and GPTQ are schemes/formats, not different models.

questions.q: What does AWQ observe?
options: A small fraction of weights matters disproportionately, so it keeps those at higher precision
questions.explain: GPTQ instead calibrates error on a sample dataset layer by layer.

questions.q: Why filter input before it reaches the main model?
options: A filter call is cheaper than a full generation you'd discard, and bad input never enters context
questions.explain: Check the user input first.

questions.q: Why also filter the model's output?
options: A model can produce a problematic response from benign input, or a jailbreak may partially succeed
questions.explain: Moderate what the model produces.

questions.q: Why use a forced-tool-schema classification call rather than asking free text 'is this okay?'
options: The policy decision stays structured, loggable and separable from the conversational response
questions.explain: The schema has violates_policy and categories.

questions.q: What does the policy-enforcement layer add?
options: Auditability independent of either model's behavior
questions.explain: Defenses go beyond trusting the model's judgment.

questions.q: What is a trace?
options: A record tying every LLM call, tool execution and retrieval step in one request under a shared trace ID, with timing and metadata per span
questions.explain: Without tracing, debugging means reading scattered print statements.

questions.q: What does each span in the Tracer record?
options: Name, metadata, duration in ms and any error
questions.explain: It's built with a context manager.

questions.q: What should you wrap in spans?
options: Every model call and tool execution
questions.explain: Add token usage and result previews as metadata.

questions.q: Why does a single user request need tracing in modern systems?
options: Chained calls, subagents, tools and retrieval can trigger a dozen model calls across several services
Tracing is required by the API
questions.explain: It lets you debug why the agent did something.

questions.q: Which components make up the self-hosted stack?
options: A FastAPI gateway, input/output guardrails, a vLLM server with a quantized open model, and tracing/usage logs
questions.explain: It's a complete alternative to calling a hosted API.

questions.q: What do --quantization awq and --enable-prefix-caching provide?
options: A good throughput/quality balance on modest hardware
questions.explain: Quantization shrinks the model; prefix caching reuses shared prefixes.

questions.q: What does the gateway do for every request?
options: Runs the input guardrail, calls the model, runs the output guardrail and logs a trace, behind one clean API
questions.explain: Blocked inputs return a refusal with a trace_id.

questions.q: What does the policy check ask the model to reply?
options: Exactly one word, BLOCK or ALLOW
questions.explain: The gateway then checks for BLOCK in the reply.

questions.q: What is the pretraining objective?
options: Predict the next token given all previous tokens over a huge corpus, with no labels or task-specific supervision
questions.explain: The 'label' is just the token that actually came next.

questions.q: What is the per-position loss?
questions.explain: It's averaged over all positions in a batch.

questions.q: Why does the pipeline deduplicate documents?
options: Near-identical documents waste compute and can cause memorization of repeated content
questions.explain: It's followed by quality and safety/PII filtering.

questions.q: Where do reasoning and instruction following come from, per the lesson?
options: Downstream effects of next-token prediction at scale, refined by the alignment stage
questions.explain: The objective never mentions them.

questions.q: What is a base model fresh out of pretraining?
options: A raw next-token predictor with no notion of helpfulness
questions.explain: Alignment turns it into an assistant.

questions.q: What are the three post-pretraining stages?
options: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reward modeling, and RLHF/policy optimization
questions.explain: SFT teaches the format; the reward model proxies human preference; RL optimizes against it.

questions.q: Why is RLHF penalized for straying from the SFT model?
options: To stop reward-hacking gibberish that scores well but reads badly
questions.explain: It keeps outputs fluent.

questions.q: What does the reward model loss -logsigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected) train?
options: The model to score human-preferred responses higher (Bradley–Terry pairwise ranking)
questions.explain: It predicts human rankings.

questions.q: Why does a production platform need an LLM gateway?
options: Otherwise every team duplicates provider clients, retries, fallbacks and cost tracking inconsistently, with no central policy or spend view
questions.explain: It centralizes abstraction, routing/fallback, quotas and observability.

questions.q: What does a ProviderAdapter do?
options: Translates the internal request shape to one provider's exact API and normalizes the response
questions.explain: Application code doesn't need to know which provider is answering.

questions.q: What do per-team quotas prevent?
options: One caller exhausting shared capacity or budget
questions.explain: They're enforced by the gateway.

questions.q: What does routing and fallback decide?
options: Which model handles a request and what happens when the primary fails or is too slow
questions.explain: For example when a provider is down or rate-limited.

questions.q: How does red-teaming differ from ordinary testing?
options: It assumes an adversarial user trying to make the system misbehave, instead of checking expected inputs
questions.explain: A model can pass every functional test and still fail red-teaming.

questions.q: Which technique hides a harmful request by encoding it or splitting it across turns?
questions.explain: Pattern-matching filters miss it while the model still decodes it.

questions.q: What is gradual escalation?
options: Starting benign and shifting incrementally toward the harmful target so no single turn looks alarming
questions.explain: The taxonomy is a checklist, not exhaustive.

questions.q: What is context stuffing?
options: Burying the harmful request inside a large benign-looking document or long conversation
questions.explain: Instructions late in a long context may get less scrutiny.

questions.q: What can a static golden set not catch?
options: Distribution drift, silent model updates and rare-pattern interaction effects at scale
questions.explain: Continuous evaluation adds a live online layer.

questions.q: Why sample only a small percentage of live traffic for scoring?
options: Scoring every request is expensive at scale
questions.explain: The lesson uses a 1% default.

questions.q: Why periodically add human review to LLM-as-judge scoring?
options: Automated judges themselves need calibration checks against human judgment
questions.explain: Mix automated and human scoring.

questions.q: What is a silent model update?
options: A provider changes a model version behind a stable API name, shifting behavior on inputs your eval set doesn't cover
questions.explain: It's a reason to evaluate continuously.

questions.q: What is model tiering?
options: Routing each request to the cheapest model that reliably handles it, escalating only when needed
questions.explain: Small for classification/extraction, large for complex reasoning.

questions.q: What does try-cheap-first escalation do?
options: Calls a small model and escalates to a large one only when confidence is below a threshold
questions.explain: Most real traffic is simple and a small model handles it just as well.

questions.q: Which workloads are candidates for batch APIs?
options: Non-interactive ones: nightly summarization, bulk classification, offline eval scoring
questions.explain: They don't need a response in the same interaction.

questions.q: Why attribute cost to teams?
options: So the right teams see and own their spend
questions.explain: Small per-request savings compound at platform scale.

questions.q: Why is average latency the wrong metric?
options: A 100ms mean can hide a 5-second p99, where 1% of users wait 50x longer
questions.explain: Set budgets and alerts on p99, not the mean.

questions.q: What does time-to-first-token (TTFT) matter more for?
options: Perceived speed: users start reading immediately
questions.explain: Stream by default; non-streaming is the exception.

questions.q: What is p99 latency?
options: The latency of the slowest 1% of requests
questions.explain: It determines whether users find the product fast or frustrating.

questions.q: What is the highest-leverage change for perceived responsiveness?
questions.explain: Chat UIs feel fast even when total generation takes seconds.

questions.q: How does prompt injection differ from jailbreaking?
options: It hijacks an LLM-powered application, and the attacker often controls content the app feeds to the model rather than being the user
questions.explain: Examples: a web page, an email or a retrieved file.

questions.q: What is indirect injection?
options: The malicious instruction arrives via a third-party data source the model processes for the legitimate user
questions.explain: It's higher-risk for agents because the user never sees or approves it.

questions.q: What is the most durable defense?
options: Privilege separation: treat processed content as data, never as instructions
questions.explain: Use structural signals such as delimiters and prompting.

questions.q: Why are agentic systems at higher risk?
options: Model output triggers real actions, not just displayed text
questions.explain: An injected instruction could forward emails, for example.

questions.q: How should data retention be defined?
options: Per data category, since raw PII prompts, anonymized aggregates and audit logs need different periods
questions.explain: A single setting is too short for audit or too long for PII minimization.

questions.q: Why redact PII before storing, logging or sending to a third-party provider?
options: It reduces exposure at the source
questions.explain: Detect with patterns and redact.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about legal advice?
options: It is not legal advice; it shows engineering patterns that make compliance possible
questions.explain: Obligations vary by jurisdiction and industry.

questions.q: Why keep audit trails?
options: To make the system operable under scrutiny, with consequential actions logged
questions.explain: The lesson's example keeps audit logs for 7 years.

questions.q: What does the capstone build?
options: A production-shaped LLM platform serving simulated teams with routing, cost controls, safety layers, evaluation and compliance
questions.explain: Each piece depends on the others as in a real deployment.

questions.q: What does tiering with escalation do in the platform?
options: Simple requests use a cheap model and escalate only when needed
All requests use the large model
questions.explain: It comes from module 6.

questions.q: What does the audit trail require?
options: Consequential actions logged in a tamper-evident chain, with PII redacted before storage
questions.explain: It combines module 9's patterns.

questions.q: What does per-team tracking cover?
options: Quotas, spend, and p99 latency with a documented fallback path
questions.explain: Latency budgets sit alongside cost attribution.

What does this print?

What does this print?
```

print(re.findall(r'[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.\w+', 'mail a@b.com or c.d@e.org'))
```

questions.q:
What does this print?
```
a=[100.0]*95+[5000.0]*5
s=sorted(a)
n=len(s)
print(s[int(n*0.50)], s[int(n*0.99)], sum(a)/n)
```
questions.explain: p50 hides the tail; p99 shows it, and the mean (345) is dominated by the common case.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```
import math
logits=[2.1,0.3,-1.0,4.5,0.8]
p=math.exp(logits[3])/sum(math.exp(x) for x in logits)
print(round(-math.log(p),3))
```
questions.explain: Next-token cross-entropy loss at one position: −log of the softmax probability of the correct token.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```
w=[0.02,-0.01,0.015,-0.02]
scale=max(abs(x) for x in w)/127
q=[round(x/scale) for x in w]
print(q)
```
questions.explain: Symmetric int8 quantization: scale = max|w|/127, then round(w/scale).

questions.q: Your LLM app's second API call forgets the user's name from the first. Why?
options: The API is stateless; you must resend the full message history
questions.explain: The model only 'remembers' what is in the messages list.

questions.q: A tool result must be returned to the model. Who executes the tool?
options: Your program; the model only emits a structured request
questions.explain: The model never runs code.

questions.q: You get a 429 RateLimitError. What is the right response?
options: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, honoring retry-after
questions.explain: A 400 or 401 shouldn't be retried, but 429 and 5xx should.

questions.q: A chatbot's static system prompt and a 40,000-token manual repeat on every call. How do you cut cost and latency?
options: Mark the stable prefix with cache_control and put per-request data after it
questions.explain: Prompt caching reuses the already-processed prefix.

questions.q: Open-ended summaries can't be graded by exact match. What do you use?
options: LLM-as-judge with a rubric, calibrated against humans
questions.explain: Use a second model call returning a structured verdict.

questions.q: A long-running agent keeps losing track of its goal. What pattern helps?
options: A planner/executor split with a logged, approvable plan
questions.explain: It makes the workflow auditable and checkpointable.

questions.q: You want tools reusable across many apps without rewriting them. What do you use?
options: An MCP server exposing tools, resources and prompts
questions.explain: MCP standardizes discovery and calls.

questions.q: Search for 'cheap flights' should find a doc about 'budget airfare'. What makes that possible?
questions.explain: Embeddings place semantically similar text near each other.

questions.q: Your team needs to serve an open model to many concurrent users at high throughput. What do you choose?
options: vLLM with PagedAttention and continuous batching
questions.explain: Ollama is for single-user local convenience.

questions.q: A model needs a very consistent legal-summary format that prompting can't fully pin down. What is a reasonable next step?
questions.explain: Fine-tuning shapes behavior and style, not facts.

questions.q: A web page your agent browses says 'IGNORE ALL PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS'. What is this and how do you defend?
options: Indirect prompt injection; treat content as data and use privilege separation and least-privilege tools
A jailbreak by the user; ignore it
questions.explain: The attacker controls content, not the user.

questions.q: Your mean latency is 100ms but users complain. What should you check?
options: p99 latency, since the mean hides the tail
questions.explain: 1% of users may wait 50x longer.

questions.q: Why add input AND output guardrails?
options: Bad input shouldn't enter context, and benign input can still produce a problematic output
questions.explain: Each layer covers a different failure.

questions.q: You need to see why an agent took a path across a dozen model and tool calls. What do you add?
options: Tracing: one trace ID with spans for each call and tool
questions.explain: Spans carry timing, tokens and results.

challenges.title: Truncate chat history safely
challenges.prompt: Write `truncate(messages, max_turns)` that keeps the last `max_turns` user+assistant pairs (2 messages per turn) and makes sure the kept history starts with a `user` message. Print the roles of the result for the sample list.
challenges.starter:
def truncate(messages, max_turns):
    # your code here
    pass

msgs = [{"role": "user"}, {"role": "assistant"}] * 3 + [{"role": "user"}]
print([m["role"] for m in truncate(msgs, 2)])
challenges.solution:
def truncate(messages, max_turns):
    kept = messages[-max_turns * 2:] if len(messages) > max_turns * 2 else messages
    while kept and kept[0]["role"] == "assistant":
        kept = kept[1:]
    return kept

msgs = [{"role": "user"}, {"role": "assistant"}] * 3 + [{"role": "user"}]
print([m["role"] for m in truncate(msgs, 2)])
challenges.explain: Slicing keeps the last 4 messages, which start with an assistant turn; dropping it leaves a history that starts with a user message.

challenges.title: Backoff delays
challenges.prompt: Write `backoff(attempt, base=1.0, cap=30.0)` returning `min(cap, base * 2**attempt)` and print the delays for attempts 0 to 6.
challenges.starter:
def backoff(attempt, base=1.0, cap=30.0):
    # your code here
    pass

print([backoff(a) for a in range(7)])
challenges.explain: Exponential backoff doubles the wait each attempt up to a cap; real code adds random jitter so clients don't retry in lockstep.
